stufe_0_frage: What tools does an electronics engineer need?
stufe_1_frage: Why does something oscillate on its own?
stufe_2_frage: How does music travel through the air?
stufe_3_frage: How do you turn a little voltage into more – without heat?
stufe_4_frage: How do you dim AC voltage?
stufe_5_frage: How much power, how much heat?
stufe_6_frage: How do you measure tiny changes?
stufe_7_frage: How does a voltage become a one?
lex_spule_hf: These small coils have only a few turns. They suit fast oscillations. The 220 µH (microhenry) antenna coil and the variable capacitor form the tuned circuit of your radio. There are also 1 mH and 10 mH coils for lower tones.
lex_drehkondensator: A variable capacitor has plates that turn into each other. The further they overlap, the larger the capacitance: from 10 to 500 pF (picofarad). Tap it and the knob appears. This is how you tune a tuned circuit.
lex_diode_ge: The germanium diode already conducts from about 0.2 volts. That is why it can pick up very weak transmitters. In the radio it turns the fast oscillation from the antenna back into sound.
lex_kristallhoerer: The crystal earpiece is an earphone without a battery. Inside it sits a thin crystal disc. When a voltage is applied, it bends a little and makes the sound. It needs almost no current. That is why the power of the transmitters is enough for it in a crystal radio.
exp3_1_1_frage: A capacitor stores charge. A coil keeps the current going. What happens when they work together?
exp3_1_1_v1: The voltage swings back and forth and gets smaller.
exp3_1_1_v2: The voltage jumps up once and then stays there.
exp3_1_1_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_1_b1: After every jump, K1 showed a wave that kept getting smaller.
exp3_1_1_b2: K1 only showed jumps, no wave.
exp3_1_1_b3: I couldn’t see anything on the screen.
exp3_1_1_s1: The generator puts out a square wave. Five times a second it jumps up and back down.
exp3_1_1_s2: Connect G through the capacitor C1 to the coil SP1. The other end of the coil goes to 0V.
exp3_1_1_s3: Put probe K1 on C2, between the capacitor and the coil. Look at the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_1_h1: Do you only see jumps? Check that the coil is plugged into C2 and 0V.
exp3_1_1_h2: Is the wave too small or too big? Change the volts per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_1_loesung: After every jump, the voltage at the coil swings back and forth. Each swing is a bit smaller than the one before. After a few swings it has almost gone.
exp3_1_1_erklaerung: At the jump, charge flows into the capacitor. The coil keeps the current going – even when the capacitor is already full. So it charges it too far. Then the charge flows back, and everything starts again. The energy swings back and forth between the capacitor and the coil. Each time, a part of it turns into heat in the coil’s wire. That is why the swing gets smaller. This is called a damped oscillation. A capacitor and a coil together are called a resonant circuit.
exp3_1_1_mehr: In the capacitor the energy sits in the electric field, in the coil in the magnetic field. Without losses the circuit would keep swinging forever. How fast it swings depends on L and C: f = 1 / (2π · √(L · C)). With 1 H and 1 µF that is about 159 Hz.
exp3_1_1_w1: Use a 100 nF capacitor instead of 1 µF. What happens to the wave?
exp3_1_1_w2: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. Compare the curves.
exp3_1_1_echt: A swing is also a pendulum like this: you push it once. Then it swings back and forth and slowly calms down. There is a resonant circuit in every radio.
exp3_1_2_frage: In the last experiment the circuit swung about 160 times a second. What happens with a smaller coil?
exp3_1_2_v1: With the smaller coil the circuit swings faster.
exp3_1_2_v2: With the smaller coil the circuit swings more slowly.
exp3_1_2_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_2_b1: With the smaller coil the waves were closer together. The frequency went up.
exp3_1_2_b2: With the smaller coil the waves were further apart.
exp3_1_2_s1: Take your circuit from the last experiment. Read the frequency on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_2_s2: Swap the 1 H coil for the 100 mH coil.
exp3_1_2_h1: The frequency is at the top of the screen, to the right of peak-to-peak.
exp3_1_2_h2: Are the waves very narrow? Choose fewer milliseconds per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_2_loesung: With 1 H the circuit swings about 159 times a second, with 100 mH about 500 times. Smaller coil – higher frequency. Bigger coil – lower frequency.
exp3_1_2_erklaerung: A big coil keeps the current going for a long time. A big capacitor takes a long time to fill up. Both make the back and forth slower. With a smaller coil it goes faster. The frequency depends on both: on the inductance L of the coil and on the capacitance C of the capacitor.
exp3_1_2_mehr: The Thomson formula is f = 1 / (2π · √(L · C)). With 100 mH and 1 µF it gives 503 Hz. The coil is ten times smaller, but the frequency is only a bit more than three times higher. That is because the formula has a square root: √10 ≈ 3.16.
exp3_1_2_w1: Use the 1 H coil again, but with a 100 nF capacitor. What do you measure?
exp3_1_2_w2: Put two 1 µF capacitors side by side. How does the frequency change?
exp3_1_2_echt: A guitar works in a similar way: a thick, heavy string swings more slowly and sounds lower than a thin one.
exp3_1_3_frage: In the coil’s wire, a part of the energy turns into heat. What happens if you add a resistor?
exp3_1_3_v2: The swinging gets faster, so it gets higher.
exp3_1_3_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_3_b1: With the resistor there were fewer waves. They got smaller faster.
exp3_1_3_b2: With the resistor the waves were closer together.
exp3_1_3_s1: Take your circuit with the 1 H coil. Count how many waves you see after a jump.
exp3_1_3_s2: Put a 330 Ω resistor between G and the capacitor.
exp3_1_3_h1: The resistor goes into the connection from G to the capacitor. Remove the old wire from G to A1.
exp3_1_3_h2: Can you hardly see any waves? Choose 2 milliseconds per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_3_loesung: Without the resistor you see many waves after every jump. With 330 Ω there are only one or two left. The frequency stays almost the same.
exp3_1_3_erklaerung: With every back and forth, the current flows through the resistor. There, a part of the energy turns into heat. The bigger the resistor, the faster the energy is used up. The swinging dies away faster. This is called damping. The frequency hardly changes.
exp3_1_3_mehr: The quality factor Q tells you how strongly a circuit is damped. For a series circuit, Q = √(L / C) / R. R is all the resistances together: the coil with 100 Ω, the generator with 50 Ω and your resistor. With 330 Ω, Q is about 2; without it, about 7. The higher the quality factor, the longer the circuit keeps ringing.
exp3_1_3_w1: Use a 1 kΩ resistor instead of 330 Ω. Does the circuit still swing?
exp3_1_3_w2: Use a 47 Ω resistor. How many waves do you count now?
exp3_1_3_echt: The shock absorbers in a car brake in exactly this way: after a bump, the car shouldn’t keep bouncing for long.
exp3_1_4_frage: A swing goes highest when you push it at the right rhythm. Is that also true for the resonant circuit?
exp3_1_4_v1: At one particular frequency the most current flows.
exp3_1_4_v2: The higher the frequency, the more current flows.
exp3_1_4_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_4_b1: At about 160 Hz the curve at K1 was biggest. Above and below it, it got smaller.
exp3_1_4_b2: The curve kept getting bigger with the frequency.
exp3_1_4_s1: Build a chain: G, 1 µF capacitor, 1 H coil, 100 Ω resistor, 0V.
exp3_1_4_s2: Put probe K1 between the coil and the resistor. The voltage at the resistor shows you how much current flows.
exp3_1_4_s3: The generator puts out a 50 Hz sine wave. Slowly turn the frequency up. Where is the curve biggest?
exp3_1_4_h1: Set the generator to the range 100 to 1000 Hz. Move the slider slowly.
exp3_1_4_h2: You will find the biggest curve near the frequency from the first experiment.
exp3_1_4_loesung: At about 159 Hz the curve is biggest: a little over 0.8 V peak-to-peak. This is also the frequency at which the circuit swings by itself. It is called the resonant frequency.
exp3_1_4_erklaerung: At low frequencies the capacitor holds back the current. At high frequencies the coil holds it back. At the resonant frequency the two cancel each other out exactly. Then only the resistors limit the current. The generator pushes the circuit exactly in time with its own swinging – just like you push a swing.
exp3_1_4_mehr: The AC resistance of the coil is X_L = 2π · f · L, that of the capacitor is X_C = 1 / (2π · f · C). At resonance both are the same size. They work against each other and cancel out. If you set X_L = X_C, you get the Thomson formula again.
exp3_1_4_w1: Swap the coil for the 100 mH coil. Where is the resonance now?
exp3_1_4_w2: Put a second probe on C2, between the capacitor and the coil. How big is the voltage there at resonance? Compare it with the generator.
exp3_1_4_echt: That is why soldiers don’t march in step across a bridge: their rhythm could make the bridge resonate.
exp3_1_5_titel: The parallel circuit as a filter
exp3_1_5_frage: Now the coil and the capacitor sit side by side. A resistor sits in front of them. Which frequencies get through?
exp3_1_5_v1: Only near one frequency does a lot of voltage arrive.
exp3_1_5_v2: All frequencies get through equally well.
exp3_1_5_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_5_b1: At about 160 Hz the curve was big. At low and high frequencies it was small.
exp3_1_5_b2: The curve was the same size at all frequencies.
exp3_1_5_s1: Connect G through a 10 kΩ resistor to C2.
exp3_1_5_s2: Put the 1 µF capacitor and the 1 H coil side by side between C2 and 0V. Put probe K1 on C2.
exp3_1_5_s3: The generator starts at 50 Hz. Slowly turn the frequency up. When is the curve biggest?
exp3_1_5_h1: The coil and the capacitor each have one end on C2 and the other on 0V.
exp3_1_5_h2: You will find the biggest curve near 160 Hz. Move the slider very slowly there.
exp3_1_5_loesung: At about 159 Hz almost 1 V peak-to-peak arrives. At 50 Hz or 500 Hz it is only about 0.07 V. The circuit lets one frequency through and keeps the others away.
exp3_1_5_erklaerung: At low frequencies the coil lets the current flow to 0V almost freely. At high frequencies the capacitor does that. Either way, hardly any voltage is left at C2. At resonance, though, the current swings back and forth between the coil and the capacitor. To the outside, the circuit blocks. Then almost all the voltage arrives. This is how a radio picks one station out of many.
exp3_1_5_mehr: For a series circuit the resistance is smallest at resonance; for a parallel circuit it is biggest. Here it is about 9 kΩ. That is why at 159 Hz the voltage is shared almost half and half between the 10 kΩ resistor and the circuit.
exp3_1_5_w1: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. Where is the peak now?
exp3_1_5_w2: Use a 1 kΩ resistor instead of 10 kΩ. How does the curve change at resonance and next to it?
exp3_1_5_echt: There is a circuit like this in every radio. When you turn the station dial, you adjust a variable capacitor. That is how you choose which frequency gets through.
exp3_1_6_frage: A radio should keep one station well apart from its neighbours. What happens if the circuit loses extra energy?
exp3_1_6_v1: The peak gets lower and wider. The circuit separates less well.
exp3_1_6_v2: The peak gets higher and narrower.
exp3_1_6_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_6_b1: With the resistor the curve at 159 Hz was smaller. At 140 Hz it was almost as big as at 159 Hz.
exp3_1_6_b2: With the resistor the curve was bigger.
exp3_1_6_s1: Take your circuit from the last experiment. Set 159 Hz. Read the peak-to-peak voltage.
exp3_1_6_s2: Set 140 Hz and read it again. Then set 159 Hz again.
exp3_1_6_s3: Put a 2.2 kΩ resistor next to the circuit: one end on C2, the other on 0V.
exp3_1_6_s4: Measure again at 159 Hz and at 140 Hz. Compare with before.
exp3_1_6_h1: The new resistor is in parallel with the coil and the capacitor. It has one end on C2 and one on 0V.
exp3_1_6_h2: Write the values down. Divide the value at 140 Hz by the value at 159 Hz.
exp3_1_6_loesung: Without the resistor: about 0.95 V at 159 Hz and 0.59 V at 140 Hz. With 2.2 kΩ: about 0.30 V and 0.27 V. The peak is lower and much wider.
exp3_1_6_erklaerung: With every back and forth, the resistor uses up a part of the energy. So the circuit doesn’t swing as strongly. It hardly prefers its own frequency to its neighbours any more. Such a circuit is called wide: it has a low quality factor. A circuit with a high quality factor has a high, narrow peak. It keeps stations well apart.
exp3_1_6_mehr: For a parallel circuit, Q = R / (2π · f · L). R is all the resistances that act in parallel with the circuit: the losses of the coil (here about 9 kΩ), the 10 kΩ resistor in front and your new resistor. Without it, Q is about 5; with 2.2 kΩ, about 1.5. The width of the peak is roughly f / Q.
exp3_1_6_w1: Use a 22 kΩ resistor instead of 2.2 kΩ. Is the peak narrow or wide then?
exp3_1_6_w2: Remove the 2.2 kΩ resistor and find the two frequencies at which the curve is only 0.67 V. How far apart are they?
exp3_1_6_echt: Good radios have circuits with a high quality factor. With cheap receivers you sometimes hear two stations at once – their circuit is too wide.
exp3_1_7_frage: In the first experiment the resonant circuit stopped after every push. Can a transistor keep it swinging forever?
exp3_1_7_v1: With the transistor the circuit keeps swinging. A smaller capacitor makes the tone higher.
exp3_1_7_v2: The circuit dies away again like in the first experiment.
exp3_1_7_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_7_b1: The tone stayed. With a smaller C1 it got higher.
exp3_1_7_b2: The tone stopped after a short time.
exp3_1_7_b3: I didn’t hear a tone or see a curve.
exp3_1_7_s1: Transistor T1 keeps the resonant circuit going. There are many parts. Build step by step.
exp3_1_7_s2: The 1 H coil gets its current through the loudspeaker. That way you can hear the circuit.
exp3_1_7_s3: Switch on. Can you hear the tone? Look at the curve at K1.
exp3_1_7_s4: Swap C1 for 470 nF, 220 nF and 100 nF one after the other. How does the tone change?
exp3_1_7_h1: No tone? Check that the main switch is on. The coil must be connected to +9V through the loudspeaker.
exp3_1_7_h2: C1 connects the collector to the emitter, C2 connects the emitter to 0V. Compare with the building plan.
exp3_1_7_loesung: The tone keeps going as long as the battery supplies current. With 1 µF it sounds at about 230 Hz, with 470 nF at about 290 Hz, with 220 nF at about 390 Hz and with 100 nF at about 540 Hz.
exp3_1_7_erklaerung: In the first experiment the circuit lost energy with every back and forth. Now the transistor adds a little energy from the battery in every beat. It gets the beat from the circuit itself: through C1 and C2, part of the swinging goes back to its emitter. This is called feedback. So the circuit keeps swinging. A circuit like this is called an oscillator. Together, C1 and C2 act like a smaller capacitor. If C1 is smaller, the tone gets higher.
exp3_1_7_mehr: This circuit is called a Colpitts oscillator. C1 and C2 are in series. Together they act like C = C1 · C2 / (C1 + C2). With two times 1 µF that is 0.5 µF. The Thomson formula then gives 225 Hz. Volta measures a little more because the transistor is connected to the circuit too. The voltage at the collector even swings above the battery’s 9 V: the coil gives back the energy it has stored.
exp3_1_7_w1: Use a 470 nF capacitor for C2. What happens to the tone?
exp3_1_7_w2: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. How high does the oscillator sound now?
exp3_1_7_echt: In every radio transmitter an oscillator with a resonant circuit makes the carrier wave – only much faster than this one.
exp3_2_2_frage: Three transmitters arrive at your antenna at the same time. How do you pick out one of them?
exp3_2_2_v1: I need three antennas for that.
exp3_2_2_v2: The tuned circuit only lets through the transmitter it is tuned to.
exp3_2_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_2_2_b1: The display at A5 always stayed the same.
exp3_2_2_b2: At three positions of the variable capacitor the display rose clearly.
exp3_2_2_s1: Plug the antenna coil from C1 to C2 and the variable capacitor from D1 to D2. Connect C1 and D1 to A2, C2 and D2 to 0V. This is your tuned circuit.
exp3_2_2_s2: Plug a 10 pF capacitor from A1 to A2. Put the transmitter station into the desk and connect ANT to A1.
exp3_2_2_s3: Plug the germanium diode from A4 to A5 (ring at A5) and connect A2 to A4. Plug a 22 kΩ resistor from E6 to E7. Connect A5 to E6 and E7 to 0V.
exp3_2_2_s4: Put a voltage display on A5. Tap the variable capacitor and turn it slowly from far left to far right. Watch the display.
exp3_2_2_h1: Turn in small steps. Each transmitter sits on just a narrow stretch.
exp3_2_2_h2: Does the display stay near 0 everywhere? Check that ANT is connected to A1 and that transmitters are on in the transmitter window.
exp3_2_2_loesung: At about 50 pF, 105 pF and 310 pF the display at A5 rises to a few tenths of a volt. These are the transmitters at 1400, 1000 and 600 kHz. In between it stays near 0.
exp3_2_2_erklaerung: The coil and the variable capacitor like to oscillate at one particular frequency. If a transmitter matches it exactly, its oscillation builds up in the circuit. The other transmitters hardly join in. The diode turns the strong oscillation into a voltage you can measure. More capacitance means the circuit oscillates more slowly. That is how you choose the transmitter.
exp3_2_2_mehr: This oscillating along is called resonance. Old radios had a big knob with a scale for it. Behind it sat exactly this kind of variable capacitor.
exp3_2_2_w1: Switch off two transmitters in the transmitter window. Can you still find the third one?
exp3_2_2_w2: Use a 100 pF capacitor instead of 10 pF. Does the circuit still separate the transmitters as well?
exp3_2_2_echt: Old battery radios contain a variable capacitor. Look inside one with an adult – only devices with batteries, never devices with a mains plug.
exp3_2_3_titel: The diode gets the sound out
exp3_2_3_frage: The display at A5 shows how strongly a transmitter arrives. But where is the sound actually hiding?
exp3_2_3_v1: The sound is in the voltage at A5. It wobbles in time with the music.
exp3_2_3_v2: The sound only appears in the loudspeaker.
exp3_2_3_b1: K1 showed a line that wobbles up and down in time with the sound.
exp3_2_3_b3: I couldn't make out anything on the screen.
exp3_2_3_s1: Take your setup from the last experiment. Tune to a transmitter with the variable capacitor.
exp3_2_3_s2: Plug probe K1 onto A5. On the oscilloscope one square lasts 2 milliseconds.
exp3_2_3_s3: Tune to all three transmitters one after the other. Compare the curves.
exp3_2_3_h1: The transmitter oscillates almost a million times a second. That is too fast for the oscilloscope in Volta. It only shows what the diode makes of it.
exp3_2_3_h2: Is the curve too small? Set fewer volts per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_2_3_loesung: At A5 the voltage wobbles by a few tenths of a volt. That is the sound. With the Morse transmitter you see long and short pieces. With the time signal a short piece comes once a second.
exp3_2_3_erklaerung: The transmitter makes its fast oscillation sometimes stronger, sometimes weaker – in time with the sound. This is called amplitude modulation. The diode only lets through one half of each oscillation. At the resistor the average is left over. It rises and falls in time with the sound. This outline is called the envelope. It is the sound.
exp3_2_3_mehr: Medium wave got its name because the waves are about 200 to 600 metres long. In the past you could hear stations from all over Europe this way – especially far at night.
exp3_2_3_w1: Use a 220 kΩ resistor instead of 22 kΩ. How does the curve change?
exp3_2_3_w2: Switch the transmitters off one by one in the transmitter window. Which curve belongs to which transmitter?
exp3_2_3_echt: A real transmitter needs a licence from the state. That is why the transmitter station only exists here in Volta.
exp3_2_4_frage: A radio with no battery at all – can that work?
exp3_2_4_v1: No. Without a battery there is no sound.
exp3_2_4_v2: Yes. The power comes from the transmitter through the antenna.
exp3_2_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_2_4_b1: I heard the transmitter in the crystal earpiece.
exp3_2_4_s1: Take your setup with the tuned circuit and the diode. You don't need a battery.
exp3_2_4_s2: Plug the crystal earpiece from C6 to C7. Connect A5 to C6 and C7 to 0V. The resistor stays next to it.
exp3_2_4_s3: Switch on the app's sound. Turn the variable capacitor until you hear a transmitter.
exp3_2_4_h1: Can't hear anything? Check that the app's sound is on and that the display at A5 is high.
exp3_2_4_h2: The resistor lets the earpiece go again after each wave. Without it the sound is dull and distorted.
exp3_2_4_loesung: With antenna, tuned circuit, diode and crystal earpiece you hear all three transmitters – with no battery at all. All the power comes from the transmitter.
exp3_2_4_erklaerung: The crystal earpiece needs almost no current. The tiny power your antenna catches is enough for it. The tuned circuit chooses the transmitter. The diode gets the sound out. The earpiece makes it audible. A radio like this is called a crystal radio.
exp3_2_4_mehr: The first radios 100 years ago were exactly such crystal radios. Instead of a diode they had a crystal with a fine wire tip. That was the detector.
exp3_2_4_w1: Take the resistor out. How does it sound now?
exp3_2_4_w2: Switch off the transmitter you are listening to in the transmitter window. What do you hear then?
exp3_2_4_echt: You can also build a real crystal radio. Ask an adult to help you. Only string the wire antenna up indoors – never outside, never during a thunderstorm and never near power lines.
